name: Primary visual cortex (V1)
function: V1 (striate cortex, approximately Brodmann area 17) lies along the banks of the calcarine sulcus. It receives LGN input and represents the contralateral visual hemifield, with central vision disproportionately represented near the occipital pole. Upper-bank cortex represents lower visual field and lower-bank cortex upper visual field.

anchors.gyrus: calcarine cortex — the banks of the calcarine fissure (cuneus above, lingual gyrus below)

clinical.findings: Unilateral V1 injury can cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia, quadrantanopia or scotoma according to extent; central vision may be spared.

Bilateral primary visual-cortex injury may cause cortical blindness with preserved pupillary light reflexes. Denial/confabulation can occur; optokinetic nystagmus may be absent or impaired, and normal pupils alone do not prove the lesion location.

name: Primary auditory cortex (A1)
function: Primary auditory cortex lies predominantly on Heschl's transverse temporal gyri within the lateral sulcus, approximately area 41. Tonotopic core regions receive MGN input. Because each ear has bilateral central projections, a unilateral cortical lesion usually does not cause complete deafness in one ear.

function: Wernicke's area is a historical label for dominant posterior temporal/perisylvian language cortex, often centered on posterior superior temporal gyrus with variably included adjacent regions. Comprehension, lexical and phonological processing depend on a distributed temporal, parietal and frontal network. Language dominance is usually left-sided but varies between individuals.

name: Primary motor cortex (M1)
function: M1 lies mainly in precentral gyrus/anterior paracentral lobule (approximately area 4). Layer V pyramidal neurons contribute to corticospinal/corticobulbar output; Betz cells are a minority of corticospinal neurons. The teaching homunculus summarizes broad contralateral effector organization, while actual representations overlap and participate in wider action networks.

name: Premotor cortex
function: Lateral premotor cortex lies anterior to M1 and is conventionally associated with lateral area 6. It contributes to preparation, selection and sensory guidance of actions through dorsal/ventral premotor and wider parietofrontal networks. It has both corticocortical and direct descending motor projections.

function: SMA occupies medial superior frontal cortex anterior to medial M1, within the conventional area 6 region. SMA/pre-SMA contribute to movement initiation, sequencing, action selection and bimanual coordination through wider motor and cognitive networks. Readiness potentials are distributed signals rather than proof of one cortical origin.

name: Entorhinal cortex
function: Entorhinal cortex occupies part of the anterior parahippocampal region and links association cortex with hippocampal formation. Layers II/III provide major dentate/CA inputs, including perforant and direct routes; hippocampal/subicular return reaches deep entorhinal layers and wider cortex. This is an interconnected memory system, not a single feedforward funnel.

function: Prefrontal cortex on the orbital surface, including lateral and medial orbital gyri. It integrates sensory, reward and affective information for value-guided decisions and behavioral adaptation, through connections with temporal/limbic and striatal systems.
